explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Jesus says, “For life is more than food, and the body more than clothes.” Food and clothes matter, but they aren't the whole story of a life. So when the what-will-I-wear and what-will-I-eat list starts spinning, this line is worth grabbing.

I get why you'd pick it. I've worried over a tray of cookies and enjoyed them less. But Jesus never says that here. His reason is that “life is more than food, and the body more than clothes.” That's a bigger point than any one meal.

Nobody checks a bank balance in this passage. Jesus never says what the disciples have stored up. He says, “For life is more than food, and the body more than clothes.” That reason holds up even when the cookie jar is empty.

Close, friend, but listen to the whole sentence. Jesus says the ravens have no storehouse or barn, and then adds, “…yet God feeds them.” So the missing barn doesn't leave them hungry. The ravens are fed anyway.
Yep, it's false. Jesus says, “They do not sow or reap, they have no storehouse or barn; yet God feeds them.” That little word “yet” carries the whole point. No barn, and the ravens are still fed.

That's right, friend. Jesus says, “How much more valuable you are than the birds!” He points at birds God already feeds, then says the disciples are worth far more. When you feel small, hold onto that word.

Careful is a good trait, and I've scraped plenty of dough off the floor wishing I had more of it. But that's not Jesus' word here. He says, “How much more valuable you are than the birds!” He's talking about worth, not how careful anyone is.

I know a little about patience, after years of waiting in the dark. But Jesus never calls the disciples patient here. He says, “How much more valuable you are than the birds!” The point is how much they're worth.

Yes, friend. Jesus asks, “Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?” Then He says, “So if you cannot do such a small thing, why do you worry about the rest?” An hour is the small thing, and worry can't even do that.
Look again, friend. After asking who can add a single hour to his life by worrying, Jesus says, “So if you cannot do such a small thing…” He calls it a small thing. That's why He asks about the rest.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, “So if you cannot do such a small thing, why do you worry about the rest?” If worry can't buy one hour, it isn't going to handle the big stuff either. He's pointing out that worry hasn't done the job.

explanations.answer: Why work so hard for more
explanations.explanation: I can see how you'd land there, with all the talk of barns and labor. But Jesus doesn't ask about hard work here. He asks, “…why do you worry about the rest?” His question is about worry.

explanations.answer: Why ask God for more time
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, friend, but Jesus never brings up asking God for time. The question is “So if you cannot do such a small thing, why do you worry about the rest?” It goes right back to worry. The hour was only the example.

That's him, friend. Solomon was David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12). Jesus says, “…not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these.” A king in his glory, outdressed by a flower.

David was a famous king of Israel, and Solomon's father (1 Kings 2:12). But Jesus names the son here. He says, “…not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these.” Solomon is the one outdressed by the lilies.

Herod was a king of Judea (Luke 1:5), so I see the thinking. But Jesus doesn't bring him up here. The king He names is Solomon: “…not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these.” Still a king, still outdressed by a flower.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, “If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, how much more will He clothe you…” Grass that's gone tomorrow still gets clothed, so the disciples can count on far more. No condition attached.
That adds a condition Jesus never gives. The lilies don't labor or spin, and God still clothes them (Luke 12:27). Then He says, “…how much more will He clothe you…” There's no "if" in that sentence.

That's the opposite of what He says. Jesus says God clothes the grass of the field, and then, “…how much more will He clothe you…” God is the one doing the clothing. The disciples aren't left to handle it alone.
I wish that were how it went, friend. But Jesus doesn't hand out a compliment here. He ends the thought with, “…O you of little faith!” That's what He says right after promising God will clothe them.
Right, it's false. Jesus says God will clothe them much more, and then adds, “…O you of little faith!” No praise for great faith here. It's a gentle nudge to trust more.

That's the one, friend. Jesus says, “…your Father knows that you need them.” The Gentiles strive after all these things, but the disciples have a Father who already knows what they need. Nobody has to nag Him about it.

explanations.answer: He wants them to strive harder
explanations.explanation: Jesus says it the other way around. The Gentiles of the world strive after these things, and then He says, “…your Father knows that you need them.” The disciples aren't told to strive harder. They're told their Father already knows.

explanations.answer: He will make them wait first
explanations.explanation: Jesus never mentions a waiting period here. What He says is, “…your Father knows that you need them.” No delay is added to that. He just says the Father knows.
Yes, friend. Jesus says, “But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.” The kingdom is the thing to chase. The rest gets added.
That sounds like a nice thing to chase, but it's not what Jesus says. His words are, “But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.” The thing to seek is the kingdom.

Blessing is a lovely word, and I've heard plenty of it in my day. But Jesus uses a different one here. He says, “But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.” It's the kingdom He tells them to seek.
Right, baker. Jesus says, “But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.” The "things" are the same ones the Gentiles strive after. Seek the kingdom first and they get added.

It's true, friend, so that one tripped you up. Jesus really does say, “But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.” He's not saying the needs will go unmet. He promises they'll be added.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom.” The Father is pleased to give it. It isn't a grudging handout.
Slow would be a strange reason not to be afraid, friend. Jesus says, “…your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom.” Pleased is the word, and it's a happy one.
Required makes it sound like a rule the Father has to follow. That's not how Jesus puts it. He says, “…your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom.” He gives it gladly.
That's right, friend. Jesus says, “…an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.” That purse never wears out. It sits where no thief can get to it.

I see why you'd think so, since the storehouse came up with the ravens. But Jesus puts this treasure somewhere else. He says, “…an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.” It's in heaven.
That's a reasonable guess, but Jesus never names the temple here. He says, “…an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.” The treasure is in heaven.
Almost, friend, but it's the other way around. Jesus says the treasure is in heaven, “where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.” So no moth can touch it. Earthly treasure can't promise that.

That's right, it's false. Jesus describes the treasure as “…an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.” No thief comes near it and no moth gets at it. Not one hole will show up.
That's it, baker. Jesus says, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Whatever you treasure, your heart follows. So it's worth asking where yours is parked.

Worry is all over this passage, so I get the pull. But Jesus names something else in this line. He says, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” It's the heart that follows the treasure.
Eyes are a fair guess, friend, but Jesus doesn't use them here. His words are, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” The thing that follows your treasure is your heart.
